questions.question: What is the water that falls from clouds in small drops called?
questions.explanation: Raindrops are not shaped like tears. Small drops are round, and big ones get flattened at the bottom as they fall.

questions.question: What do we call the soft white flakes that fall when it is very cold?
questions.explanation: Snow forms when water in clouds freezes into tiny ice crystals. The crystals stick together and make flakes.

questions.question: What is hot, melted rock called when it flows out of a volcano?
questions.explanation: Lava can be hotter than 1,000 degrees Celsius. When it cools, it turns into hard rock.

questions.question: Which season is the coldest in Denmark?
questions.explanation: In winter the days are short and the Sun is low in the sky. So the ground and air get less heat.

questions.question: What do you see in the sky when the Sun shines through rain?
questions.explanation: Sunlight bends inside the raindrops and splits into colours. You must have the Sun behind you to see it.

questions.question: What is the loud noise that follows a flash of lightning?
questions.explanation: Light travels much faster than sound, so we see the flash first and hear the bang a little later.

questions.question: What is a tornado?
questions.explanation: A tornado hangs down from a storm cloud and can lift things off the ground. Most last only a few minutes.

questions.question: What do we call a huge tropical storm with strong winds and heavy rain over the sea?
questions.explanation: Hurricanes get their energy from warm sea water. They get weaker when they move over land or cold water.

questions.question: What is the outer layer of the Earth, where we live, called?
questions.explanation: The crust is thin compared with the rest of the Earth, like the skin of an apple.

questions.question: What is the very middle of the Earth called?
questions.explanation: The core is about as hot as the surface of the Sun. It starts almost 3,000 km below our feet.

questions.question: What do we call balls of ice that fall from storm clouds?
questions.explanation: Strong rising winds in a storm cloud hold the hailstones up while more ice freezes onto them. Some grow as big as golf balls.

questions.question: What is fog?
questions.correct: A cloud close to the ground
questions.explanation: Fog is made of tiny water drops, just like a cloud. If you walk into fog on a hill, you are inside a cloud.

questions.question: What do we put on a roof to show which way the wind blows?
questions.explanation: The pointer of a weather vane turns until it faces into the wind. Many old vanes are shaped like cockerels.

questions.question: Which tool do we use to measure how hot or cold the air is?
questions.explanation: A thermometer shows the temperature in degrees. In Denmark we use degrees Celsius.

questions.question: Which tool measures how much rain has fallen?
questions.explanation: A simple rain gauge is a container with a scale on the side. It shows how many millimetres of rain have fallen.

questions.question: How many sides does a snowflake usually have?
questions.explanation: Water molecules freeze into a six-sided pattern. That is why snowflakes have six arms or six corners.

questions.question: Which light rock from volcanoes can float on water?
questions.explanation: Pumice is full of tiny holes made by gas bubbles in the lava. The holes make it so light that it floats.

questions.question: What do we call it when the ground shakes suddenly?
questions.explanation: Earthquakes happen when big pieces of the Earth's crust slip past each other and the rock suddenly moves.

questions.question: What do we call the way water moves from sea to sky to land and back again?
questions.explanation: The Sun warms the sea and the water rises as vapour. It makes clouds, falls as rain and runs back to the sea.

questions.question: What do we call it when the Sun warms water and it rises into the air as invisible gas?
questions.explanation: This is why puddles slowly disappear after the rain stops. The water has not gone away. It is in the air.

questions.question: What are clouds made of?
questions.correct: Tiny drops of water and ice
questions.explanation: The drops are so small and light that they float in the air. They only fall when they join and get heavy.

questions.question: What do we call a long time with little or no rain?
questions.explanation: During a drought, rivers and lakes get low and plants dry up. Farmers can struggle to grow food.

questions.question: What do we call it when too much water covers land that is normally dry?
questions.explanation: Floods can happen after heavy rain, when snow melts fast, or when the sea rises in a storm.

questions.question: What is a heavy snowstorm with strong wind called?
questions.explanation: In a blizzard the wind blows the snow around, so it is hard to see anything even a few metres away.

questions.question: In which season do the leaves on many trees turn red and yellow and fall off?
questions.explanation: Trees stop making green colour when the days get shorter. Then the red and yellow colours show up.

questions.question: Which smooth, shiny stone, often white, do sculptors use for statues?
questions.explanation: Marble is easy to carve and polishes well. Many famous statues from Greece and Rome are made of it.

questions.question: What is lightning?
questions.explanation: Lightning is a huge spark that jumps inside a cloud or between a cloud and the ground. It is about five times hotter than the Sun's surface.

questions.question: What are the tiny drops of water you find on grass in the early morning?
questions.explanation: At night, grass and leaves get cold. Water vapour in the air turns into drops on them.

questions.question: What do we call the opening at the top of a volcano?
questions.explanation: Lava, ash and gas come out of the crater when a volcano erupts.

questions.question: Which clear gem is the hardest mineral found in nature?
questions.explanation: Diamonds form deep in the Earth, where it is very hot and the pressure is huge. Only another diamond can scratch a diamond.

questions.question: What do we call the layer of air around the Earth?
questions.explanation: The atmosphere gives us air to breathe and protects us from much of the Sun's harmful light.

questions.question: What do we call a report that says what the weather will be like tomorrow?
questions.explanation: Forecasters use satellites, computers and measurements from all over the world to work out what the weather will do.

questions.question: Which soft white rock was used to write on blackboards?
questions.explanation: Chalk is so soft that tiny bits rub off as you write, leaving a white line on the dark board.

questions.question: Which black rock do people dig up and burn for heat and power?
questions.explanation: Coal is dug out of mines deep underground or from huge open pits. When it burns, it gives off heat and smoke.

questions.question: What do we call a giant sea wave made by an earthquake under the sea?
questions.explanation: A tsunami can cross a whole ocean. Near the coast it grows tall and rushes onto the land.

questions.question: Which kind of climate is hot and wet all year, with rainforests?
questions.explanation: Rainforests grow near the equator. The Sun is high in the sky all year, so it is always warm, and in many places it rains almost every day.

questions.question: What do we call hot water that shoots high into the air from a hole in the ground?
questions.explanation: Water deep underground is heated by hot rock until it boils and bursts up. Then the hole fills with water again, and it all happens once more.

questions.question: What do we call the tiny white ice crystals on grass and windows on a very cold morning?
questions.explanation: Frost forms when water vapour turns straight into ice on a surface colder than 0 degrees.

questions.question: What is sand mostly made from?
questions.explanation: Wind, water and ice slowly break rock into smaller and smaller pieces. Some white beaches are made of broken shells and coral instead.

questions.question: What do we call a mountain with an opening where hot rock can come out?
questions.explanation: Volcanoes form where hot melted rock from deep in the Earth finds a way up to the surface.

questions.question: Which type of cloud looks like white cotton-wool puffs on a fine day?
questions.explanation: Cumulus means 'heap' in Latin. If it grows very tall and dark, it can turn into a storm cloud.

questions.question: What do we call it when wind, water or ice carry away bits of soil and rock?
questions.explanation: Over millions of years, erosion by rivers and glaciers can carve out deep valleys and canyons.

questions.question: What does a barometer measure?
questions.explanation: When air pressure falls, bad weather is often coming. Old sailors watched their barometers closely.

questions.question: Which black, glassy rock forms when lava cools very fast?
questions.explanation: People in the Stone Age made sharp knives and arrow tips from obsidian, because it breaks into very sharp edges.

questions.question: What do we call a mix of rain and snow falling together?
questions.explanation: Sleet happens when snow melts a little as it falls through warmer air near the ground.

questions.question: In weather forecasts, what is a 'front'?
questions.correct: Where warm and cold air meet
wrong: A line of tall clouds at sea
The first rain of a storm
A calm area of high air
questions.explanation: Fronts often bring clouds, rain and a change in temperature when they pass over.

questions.question: Which layer of the Earth lies between the crust and the core?
questions.explanation: The mantle makes up most of the Earth's volume. It is solid, hot rock, but over millions of years it flows very slowly.

questions.question: What is the pool of melted rock under a volcano called?
questions.explanation: Magma is called lava once it reaches the surface. A chamber can lie several kilometres underground.

questions.question: Which two metals mostly make up the Earth's core?
questions.explanation: Iron and nickel are heavy, so they sank to the middle when the Earth was young and melted.

questions.question: What are the huge, slowly moving pieces of the Earth's crust called?
questions.explanation: The plates move a few centimetres a year, about as fast as your fingernails grow.

questions.question: Where do most earthquakes happen?
questions.correct: Along the edges of tectonic plates
questions.explanation: At plate edges, the plates push, pull or slide past each other. Sometimes they get stuck and then slip suddenly.

questions.question: Which ocean is surrounded by the 'Ring of Fire', a belt of volcanoes and earthquakes?
questions.explanation: The ring follows the edges of the plates around the Pacific. Japan, Chile and New Zealand all lie on it.

questions.question: What kind of rock forms when magma or lava cools and hardens?
questions.explanation: The word igneous comes from the Latin word for fire. Granite and basalt are both igneous rocks.

questions.question: Marble is a rock made when heat and pressure change which other rock?
questions.explanation: Marble is metamorphic, which means 'changed form'. Pure limestone turns into white marble.

questions.question: What is chalk mostly made from?
questions.explanation: Most chalk formed on the sea floor while dinosaurs lived. The Cretaceous period is named after chalk, which is 'creta' in Latin.

questions.question: In a cave, what do we call the icicle-shaped rock that hangs down from the ceiling?
questions.explanation: A stalactite grows from the ceiling. A stalagmite grows up from the floor. Remember: stalaCtites hang from the Ceiling.

questions.question: Which mineral is the softest on the Mohs hardness scale?
questions.explanation: Talc is so soft you can scratch it with a fingernail. It feels smooth and greasy, a bit like soap.

questions.question: Which mineral is the main part of most beach sand?
questions.explanation: Quartz is very hard and does not break down easily, so it stays behind when softer minerals wear away.

questions.question: Coal formed mainly from what?
questions.explanation: Plants in warm swamp forests died and got buried. Over millions of years, heat and pressure turned them into coal.

questions.question: In which layer of the atmosphere does our weather happen?
questions.explanation: The troposphere is the lowest layer, with most of the air and nearly all the clouds. It is thicker over the equator than over the poles.

questions.question: What does the ozone layer do?
wrong: It keeps the ground warm at night
questions.explanation: Ultraviolet light from the Sun can harm skin and eyes. The ozone layer soaks up the most dangerous kinds.

questions.question: What is the weather like in the very centre of a hurricane?
questions.explanation: The calm centre is called the eye. It is surrounded by the eyewall, where the winds are strongest.

questions.question: What does humidity tell us?
questions.correct: How much water vapour is in the air
questions.explanation: On a humid day the air feels sticky, because sweat dries more slowly from your skin.

questions.question: Which instrument measures wind speed?
questions.explanation: Many anemometers have three small cups that spin faster when the wind is stronger.

questions.question: What does a seismograph record?
questions.explanation: Seismographs pick up shaking from earthquakes, even from very far away on the other side of the world.

questions.question: You see lightning, then count 3 seconds before you hear thunder. How far away is the strike?
questions.explanation: Sound travels about 1 kilometre in 3 seconds. Light is so fast that you see the flash almost at once.

questions.question: Which scale measures wind strength, from calm to hurricane force?
questions.explanation: It is named after Francis Beaufort, an officer in the British navy, who drew it up for sailors in 1805.

questions.question: What is a monsoon?
questions.correct: A seasonal wind that brings heavy rain
wrong: A fast spinning column of air
A wave caused by an earthquake
questions.explanation: Monsoon winds change direction with the seasons. In South Asia, the summer monsoon brings most of the year's rain.

questions.question: What makes the wind blow?
questions.correct: Air moving from high to low pressure
wrong: The Moon pulling on the air
The Earth's core giving off heat
questions.explanation: Warm air rises, so air pressure is lower there. Cooler air flows in to fill the gap, and we feel it as wind.

questions.question: Which climate zone is Denmark in?
questions.explanation: In temperate zones the seasons change through the year and it is neither very hot nor very cold.

questions.question: What is a savanna?
questions.correct: A grassland with wet and dry seasons
wrong: A cold plain with no trees
questions.explanation: Savannas, like those in East Africa, have scattered trees and tall grass. Many large animals graze there.

questions.question: What is permafrost?
questions.correct: Ground that stays frozen for years
wrong: Ice floating on the Arctic Sea
A very cold wind from the north
A thick layer of winter fog
questions.explanation: Permafrost covers much of the far north, such as Siberia, Alaska and northern Canada.

questions.question: What do we call a volcano that scientists expect never to erupt again?
questions.explanation: A dormant volcano is only sleeping and may wake up again. An extinct one has lost its supply of magma.

questions.question: Hailstones grow inside which kind of cloud?
questions.explanation: Cumulonimbus clouds are tall storm clouds. Strong rising winds inside them hold the hailstones up while more ice freezes on.

questions.question: Which type of cloud is thin and wispy and found very high up?
questions.explanation: Cirrus clouds are made of ice crystals. Sometimes they are the first sign that bad weather is on the way.

questions.question: Which Danish island is known for its cliffs of hard granite?
questions.explanation: Most of Denmark is covered by clay, sand and gravel left by the ice ages. On Bornholm, ancient hard rock comes up to the surface.

questions.question: What causes the sound of thunder?
questions.correct: Air heated very fast by lightning
questions.explanation: A lightning bolt heats the air around it in a split second. The air expands fast and makes a shock wave we hear as thunder.

questions.question: What is smog?
questions.correct: Fog or haze made worse by pollution
wrong: A thin kind of morning frost
Warm mist rising off the sea
questions.explanation: The word comes from 'smoke' and 'fog'. It is worst in cities with lots of traffic and little wind.

questions.question: Why is it usually colder high up on a mountain?
wrong: The Sun is much further away
There is no wind to bring warmth
questions.explanation: The Sun warms the ground, and the ground warms the air above it. As air rises, the pressure falls, so the air spreads out and cools.

questions.question: In which layer of the atmosphere is the ozone layer found?
questions.explanation: The ozone layer lies about 15 to 35 km up, well above the height where planes usually fly.

questions.question: What is the boundary between the Earth's crust and mantle called?
questions.explanation: Moho is short for Mohorovičić, the Croatian scientist who found it in 1909. Earthquake waves change speed there.

questions.question: Which scientist put forward the idea of continental drift in 1912?
questions.explanation: Wegener saw that South America and Africa fit like puzzle pieces. Most scientists only accepted his idea decades later.

questions.question: About 300 million years ago almost all land was joined in one supercontinent. What was it called?
questions.explanation: Pangaea means 'all earth'. It broke apart slowly, and the pieces drifted to where our continents are now.

questions.question: What is a caldera?
questions.correct: Basin left by a collapsed volcano
wrong: A steep cone built of ash
A crack where lava leaks out
questions.explanation: A caldera forms when a magma chamber empties and the ground above falls in. Some calderas are many kilometres wide.

questions.question: What is a pyroclastic flow?
questions.correct: A fast, hot cloud of gas and ash
questions.explanation: Pyroclastic flows can race down a volcano at well over 100 km an hour. They are far more dangerous than slow lava flows.

questions.question: Which group of minerals is the most common in the Earth's crust?
questions.explanation: Feldspars are found in granite, basalt and many other rocks. Quartz is common too, but there is much less of it.

questions.question: What is a lahar?
questions.correct: A flow of mud and volcanic ash
questions.explanation: Lahars happen when rain or melted ice mixes with loose ash on a volcano. They flow quickly down river valleys.

questions.question: Which type of volcano has wide, gentle slopes because its lava is very runny?
questions.explanation: Hawaii's Mauna Loa is a shield volcano. The name comes from the shape, like a warrior's shield lying on the ground.

questions.question: Which scale rates an earthquake by the shaking and damage people see and feel?
questions.explanation: The Mercalli scale uses numbers in Roman numerals, from I (hardly felt) to XII (total destruction).

questions.question: Which earthquake waves reach a seismograph first?
questions.explanation: P stands for primary. These waves are the fastest. S waves, the secondary ones, come next.

questions.question: Earthquake S waves cannot pass through which layer of the Earth?
questions.explanation: S waves cannot move through liquid. Their shadow told scientists that the outer core must be melted metal.

questions.question: What do we call a plate boundary where two plates slide past each other?
questions.explanation: Plates at transform boundaries get stuck and then slip, which causes earthquakes, such as along the San Andreas Fault.

questions.question: Which soft mineral is the main material in plasterboard?
questions.explanation: Gypsum is heated to make plaster. A fingernail can scratch it, because it scores only 2 on the Mohs scale.

questions.question: Slate forms when heat and pressure change which soft sedimentary rock?
questions.explanation: Slate splits into thin, flat sheets, which is why people use it for roof tiles.

questions.question: Rubies and sapphires are both forms of which mineral?
questions.explanation: Corundum scores 9 on the Mohs scale, just below diamond. A little chromium gives ruby its red colour.

questions.question: On the Mohs scale of hardness, quartz scores about what?
questions.explanation: Mohs hardness runs from 1 to 10. Quartz at 7 is harder than glass and most steel, so it can scratch both.

questions.question: What name is given to the fast winds that blow high up in the atmosphere and steer weather systems?
questions.explanation: Jet streams blow about 10 km up. Planes flying from west to east can ride them to save time and fuel.

questions.question: What do we call a warm, dry wind that flows down the lee side of the Alps?
questions.explanation: The Föhn can raise the temperature by 10 degrees or more in a few hours. It can melt snow very fast.

questions.question: In the Northern Hemisphere, the Earth's spin bends winds and ocean currents to which side?
questions.explanation: This bending is the Coriolis effect. It makes large storms such as hurricanes spin anticlockwise in the north and clockwise in the south.

questions.question: What did sailors call the calm, windless area near the equator?
questions.explanation: Sailing ships could get stuck there for days or even weeks. The phrase 'in the doldrums' also means feeling bored or low.

questions.question: What is the dew point?
questions.explanation: If air cools below its dew point, the water vapour turns into drops. That is how dew, fog and clouds form.

questions.question: Which Greek thinker wrote 'Meteorologica', an early book about the weather?
questions.explanation: Aristotle wrote it about 2,300 years ago. It covers rain, wind and thunder, and even earthquakes.

questions.question: What does 'El Niño' mean in Spanish?
questions.explanation: Fishermen in Peru saw that the warm water often arrived around Christmas, so they named it after the Christ child.

questions.question: Which scale rates tornadoes by the damage they cause?
questions.explanation: The scale is named after Ted Fujita, a Japanese-American scientist. It goes from F0 (light damage) to F5 (extreme).

questions.question: Which thin, high cloud sheet can make a ring of light around the Sun or Moon?
questions.explanation: The ring, called a halo, is made as sunlight bends through ice crystals in the cloud.

questions.question: Which type of cloud has a smooth, lens or saucer shape and forms near mountains?
questions.explanation: Lenticular clouds form when moist air flows over mountains in waves. They often seem to hover in one place.

questions.question: Where do most lightning flashes happen?
wrong: From a cloud to the ground
From the ground to a cloud
questions.explanation: Only about one flash in four reaches the ground. Most stay in the sky, where we often just see a flicker.

questions.question: In the lower atmosphere, how much does the air temperature fall for each kilometre you climb?
questions.explanation: So if it is 20 °C at sea level, the air about 3 km up is near freezing. That is why high mountain tops are often snowy.

questions.question: What is a 'rain shadow'?
questions.correct: A dry area behind a mountain range
wrong: The dark shadow of a rain cloud
Light drizzle that falls at night
questions.explanation: Wet air loses its rain as it rises over the mountains. The air that comes down the other side is dry.

questions.question: Which dark volcanic rock makes up most of the crust under the oceans?
questions.explanation: Continents are made largely of lighter, granite-like rock. Ocean crust is thinner and heavier for its size.

questions.question: What is it called when one tectonic plate slides under another?
questions.explanation: Subduction often makes deep ocean trenches and lines of volcanoes. It also causes some of the largest earthquakes.

questions.question: Cave stalactites are mostly made of which mineral?
questions.explanation: Water with dissolved limestone drips from the ceiling. Each drop leaves a tiny bit of calcite behind.

questions.question: Amber, which people find on Danish beaches, is the hardened remains of what?
questions.explanation: Some Baltic amber is about 40 million years old. It sometimes holds trapped insects.

questions.question: Who invented the mercury barometer in 1643?
questions.explanation: Torricelli, who had worked with Galileo, filled a glass tube with mercury. He saw that air pressure held the mercury up.

questions.question: Which process breaks rock into smaller pieces without moving them away?
questions.explanation: Frost, heat, rain and plant roots all weather rock. Water that freezes in a crack swells and pushes the rock apart.

questions.question: The 'Year Without a Summer' in 1816 followed an eruption of which volcano?
questions.explanation: Tambora, in Indonesia, erupted in 1815. Its gas and ash spread around the world and dimmed the sunlight, and harvests failed in many parts of Europe.

questions.question: Which Dane is seen as a founder of geology for saying that lower rock layers are older?
questions.explanation: Steno worked in the 1600s. His idea is that new layers form on top of old ones, which helps us read Earth's history.

questions.question: Which scientist found in 1936 that the Earth has a solid inner core?
questions.explanation: Inge Lehmann was a Danish earthquake scientist. She saw that some earthquake waves were bent by something deep inside the liquid core.
